paras: The threatened lynching of Daniel Smith was an outbreak of public excitement and talk of lynching in Wayne County, Indiana, in January 1882, after Smith confessed to killing his father, the farmer David H. Smith. Smith, his mother and his brother were held in the county jail at Richmond, and no crowd is reported to have moved against them. Wire services carried the case widely as a "patricide," and a later feature said the son had "narrowly escaped lynching"; no paper stated the race of anyone involved.

David H. Smith, a farmer described as 65 years old, lived near Washington in Wayne County, about fourteen miles north of Centreville, and disappeared early in January 1882. Neighbors quoted in a Washington dispatch said he had been "habitually mistreated" by his wife and sons. The Vermont Phoenix later described a long "feud" in the family, a dispute after Daniel traded one of his father's horses without his knowledge, and public threats by Daniel to kill his father.

Suspecting foul play, neighbors searched the farm on Saturday, January 14, in a party the Omaha Daily Bee put at sixty men. They found Smith's body at the bottom of a well, covered with stones, with two bullet holes in the head. The younger children said they had heard shots about the time their father vanished, and Daniel was reported to have fainted when the body was brought in while his mother "was not moved."

Susan Smith and her sons Daniel and Jacob were arrested, and on the way to jail Daniel said he alone had shot his father in a quarrel over a horse he had sold, then broke his skull with a hammer and threw the body in the well. His mother then stated that she and her sons had planned the killing and that Daniel's claim to have acted alone was meant to save her and his brother "from the gallows." A dispatch from Centreville dated January 16 reported that excitement over the murder was at "fever heat" and that lynching was "freely talked of." None of the reports describes a crowd gathering at the jail or any attempt on the prisoners.

On February 3 the Vermont Phoenix reported that the three were "safely lodged in the county jail at Richmond," that the community was "still excited over the crime," and that Daniel had "narrowly escaped lynching." A coroner's investigation was under way on January 16; its finding does not appear in the coverage. No report of an indictment or trial was found, although an August 1882 roundup of family killings in the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic listed "Dan Smith, aged 19," as having killed his father at Richmond.

The story broke on January 17 in Cincinnati and Richmond specials, under headlines such as "Heartless Patricide" in the Portland Daily Press, "Murdered His Father" in the Washington Evening Star and "A Son Confesses a Murder to Save His Mother" in the St. Paul Daily Globe. The Memphis Daily Appeal credited the confession text to a special to the Cincinnati Times-Star; versions ran from Pennsylvania to Wyoming, and one-line items appeared in weekly columns into late January. Coverage dwelt on the son's confession and the mother's composure, presenting the case as a family crime and never naming the Smiths' race.

The lynch talk itself drew only a line: the Omaha Daily Bee's Centreville dispatch mentioned it without comment, and the Vermont Phoenix feature "The Story of a Crime" closed by remarking that the "unnatural son" had narrowly escaped lynching.

The St. Paul Daily Globe reported two bullet holes in the head, while the Cambria Freeman reported five head wounds. By contrast, the Vermont Phoenix said Smith was shot three times and the Omaha Daily Bee said seven. The Vermont Phoenix also dated the killing January 16, the date of the first dispatches, which had Smith disappearing on January 4 and found on January 14.

Daniel Smith first said he acted alone, while his mother said all three had planned the killing and Jacob said he was away when it happened. Most dispatches placed the farm near Washington, Wayne County, but the Vermont Phoenix put it near Richmond and the Cambria Freeman near Hagerstown.

info: David H. Smith disappeared about January 4, 1882; his body was found Saturday, January 14; the confessions followed January 16-17; lynch talk was reported from Centreville on January 16.
Smith farm near Washington, Wayne County, Indiana, about fourteen miles north of Centreville; the accused were held in the county jail at Richmond. One brief places it near Hagerstown, Ind.
Daniel (Dan) Smith, son of David H. Smith, was the object of the lynch talk; no paper gives his race. His mother Susan Smith and brother Jacob were jailed with him.
Accused of, and confessed to, killing his father David H. Smith by shooting him and striking him with a hammer, then throwing the body in a well; his mother said she and both sons had planned it.
Not identified: residents around Centreville and the Smith neighborhood among whom lynching was 'freely talked of'.
Daniel Smith was not lynched; he was still in jail at Richmond in early February. No report of a trial was found.
